# Peripartum Cardiomyopathy: A Narrative Review

## Introduction and definition

Peripartum cardiomyopathy (PPCM) is an idiopathic, pregnancy-associated cardiomyopathy that presents with heart failure secondary to left ventricular (LV) systolic dysfunction toward the end of pregnancy or in the months following delivery, in the absence of another identifiable cause [1]. The most widely applied contemporary definition is that of the 2010 Heart Failure Association (HFA) of the European Society of Cardiology (ESC) Working Group, which characterises PPCM as a diagnosis of exclusion with an LV ejection fraction (LVEF) generally below 45% [2]. In 2010, the Study Group of the HFA defined PPCM as an idiopathic cardiomyopathy occurring towards the end of pregnancy or in the months following delivery, abortion or miscarriage, without other causes for heart failure, and with an LVEF below 45% [3]. The earlier National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute criteria additionally specified onset within the last month of pregnancy or the first five months postpartum, together with echocardiographic LV dysfunction [4].

## Epidemiology

The incidence of PPCM varies markedly by geography and ethnicity, reflecting both socioeconomic and genetic factors [5]. Reported rates range from roughly 1 in 1,000 live births in parts of South Africa to approximately 1 in 2,000 deliveries in the United States [6,7]. In a US nationwide analysis, the reported incidence of PPCM in the United States varies widely, and limited information was available on temporal trends in incidence and outcomes, with the study documenting a rising incidence over the study period [8]. The disorder remains the leading non-obstetric cause of perinatal morbidity and mortality, and up to 78% of cardiac fatalities have no known pre-existing cardiovascular disease [9].

## Pathophysiology

The pathogenesis of PPCM is incompletely understood, but a vascular/hormonal hypothesis now predominates. Recent data suggest a central role of unbalanced peri-/postpartum oxidative stress that triggers the proteolytic cleavage of the nursing hormone prolactin into a potent antiangiogenic, proapoptotic, and proinflammatory 16-kDa fragment [10]. This concept was established in a landmark study showing that female mice with a cardiomyocyte-specific deletion of stat3 develop PPCM, with enhanced cathepsin D generating a cleaved 16-kDa prolactin fragment; treatment with bromocriptine prevented disease, whereas forced generation of 16-kDa prolactin recapitulated the cardiac phenotype [11]. The antiangiogenic 16-kDa prolactin, cleaved from standard 23-kDa prolactin under unbalanced oxidative stress, is recognised as a main trigger, damaging cardiomyocytes via microRNA-146a and the NF-κB pathway [12]. An anti-angiogenic milieu, including soluble fms-like tyrosine kinase-1 (sFlt-1), links PPCM mechanistically to pre-eclampsia [13]. A systematic review confirmed a strong epidemiological association, in which pre-eclampsia is frequently cited as a risk factor and recent research suggests that pre-eclampsia and PPCM share mechanisms contributing to their pathobiology [14].

A genetic predisposition is also well established. Sequencing of dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM)-associated genes in women with PPCM revealed that 26 distinct rare truncating variants were identified in eight genes; the prevalence of truncating variants (15%) was significantly higher than in a reference population, and two-thirds were in TTN, seen in 10% of patients [15]. Subsequent work confirmed that approximately 10% of women with PPCM harbour truncating variants in TTN, while whether mutations in other genes predispose to PPCM was not known [16]. Given this overlap, genetic testing is increasingly advocated, although many variants, especially truncating variants in TTN, are poorly penetrant, limiting predictive screening of asymptomatic women [17].

## Clinical presentation and diagnosis

Symptoms—dyspnoea, fatigue and peripheral oedema—overlap with normal late pregnancy, so a high index of suspicion is essential [18]. A high index of suspicion is required not to miss the diagnosis, and measurement of natriuretic peptides, electrocardiography and echocardiography are recommended to promptly diagnose or exclude heart failure/PPCM [19]. Diagnosis remains one of exclusion, with important differentials including pulmonary embolism, myocardial infarction, hypertensive heart disease, and pre-existing cardiomyopathy [3]. International characterisation has been advanced by the EURObservational Research Programme (EORP) worldwide registry [20], which generated detailed data on patient characteristics [21] and reported clinical presentation, management and 6-month outcomes across a multinational cohort [22].

## Management

Treatment combines guideline-directed heart failure therapy with attention to pregnancy and lactation. Several studies describe signaling mechanisms mediating the deleterious action of the 16-kDa prolactin fragment and support the beneficial effects of treatment with dopamine D2 agonists in patients with PPCM [23]. The first multicentre randomised trial of bromocriptine demonstrated that LVEF improved in short- and long-term groups by 21% and 24% respectively, with the difference between groups not reaching statistical significance [24]. Because of thrombotic risk, anticoagulation is recommended alongside bromocriptine, and care is best delivered by a multidisciplinary "pregnancy heart team" as emphasised in the 2018 ESC guidelines [25,26]. The seminal 2007 mechanistic study likewise showed that prolactin inhibition prevented experimental disease [27]. Mechanical circulatory support and transplantation are reserved for refractory cardiogenic shock.

## Prognosis

Outcomes are heterogeneous. In the prospective North American IPAC study, 100 women with PPCM were followed through 1 year postpartum, with LVEF assessed by echocardiography at baseline and at 2, 6 and 12 months [28]; event-free survival at 1 year was 93%, transplant-free survival was 95%, and at 12 months 72% achieved an LVEF ≥50% [29]. Lower baseline LVEF, greater LV end-diastolic dimension, and Black race predicted poorer recovery. Selenium deficiency and autoimmune mechanisms have also been proposed as contributory factors in certain populations [30]. Subsequent pregnancies carry a substantial risk of relapse, particularly when LV function has not normalised, underscoring the need for counselling and long-term follow-up.

## Conclusion

PPCM is a potentially life-threatening but frequently reversible form of heart failure. Advances in understanding the prolactin/angiogenic axis and shared genetic predisposition with DCM have refined diagnosis and introduced disease-specific therapy, yet diagnostic delay and outcome inequity persist worldwide. Prospective registries and randomised trials remain essential to optimise care.
